title: China Escalates Scarborough Shoal Standoff With Combat Drills and New Fishing Ban
excerpt: Beijing conducted joint naval and air exercises around the disputed atoll and issued new regulations for its self-declared nature reserve, drawing no immediate response from Manila.
body:
• China's PLA Southern Theater Command conducted joint air and naval combat drills around Scarborough Shoal on August 1, calling them a response to unnamed countries undermining regional stability.
  • Beijing simultaneously issued new administrative regulations for the Huangyan Island National Nature Reserve, banning unauthorised fishing, mining, and coral extraction.
  • The China Coast Guard announced it will set up regular law enforcement patrols around the reserve and hold violators legally accountable.
  • The moves follow recent joint US-Philippine naval exercises near the shoal and come amid intensifying sovereignty disputes in the South China Sea.

The Drills

China's military conducted joint air and naval combat drills around the disputed Scarborough Shoal in the South China Sea on Saturday, the People's Liberation Army Southern Theater Command said in a statement. The exercises, held in the airspace and waters around the shoal — which China calls Huangyan Dao — were described as a necessary response to actions by "certain countries" that Beijing said were undermining regional peace and stability.

The Chinese military did not name any countries, but Scarborough Shoal is also claimed by the Philippines, where it is known as Bajo de Masinloc. The drills were designed to "test and improve the combat readiness of China's forces to defend national territorial sovereignty and maritime rights," according to the statement.

New Nature Reserve Rules

In a coordinated move, China issued a new administrative policy on Saturday for the Huangyan Island National Nature Reserve — established in September 2025, a step the Philippines denounced as a "clear pretext for occupation." Under the new regulations, unauthorised fishing, mining, coral or giant clam extraction, and other activities deemed harmful will be banned, state news agency Xinhua reported.

Violators will be "held legally accountable," Xinhua said. The China Coast Guard announced separately that it had conducted a rights-protection and law enforcement drill near the island and would strengthen its control measures in surrounding waters.

"Such patrols serve as an effective countermeasure to cope with all sorts of rights-violation and provocative acts."

— PLA Southern Theater Command spokesperson

Context and Escalation

Saturday's drills came after a pattern of tit-for-tat manoeuvres between China and the US-Philippines alliance. Just last week, China's military said it conducted a routine patrol after accusing the Philippines of "rallying foreign countries to organise so-called joint patrols, disrupting the South China Sea and undermining regional peace and stability."

The Philippine embassy in Beijing did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the latest Chinese military exercises.

China claims sovereignty over almost the entire South China Sea despite overlapping claims by several Southeast Asian nations. It rejects a 2016 arbitral ruling that invalidated its expansive territorial claims. The dispute has become one of Asia's most consequential geopolitical flashpoints, with implications for global shipping lanes and regional security architecture.

What India Is Watching

New Delhi has consistently backed freedom of navigation in the South China Sea and has growing strategic ties with the Philippines and Vietnam. For India, China's assertiveness at Scarborough is part of a broader pattern that includes border tensions along the Line of Actual Control. The Xi Jinping visit expected for the BRICS summit in India adds another layer of diplomatic complexity.

What's Next

The new nature reserve regulations signal that Beijing intends to formalise its control over the shoal through administrative and legal mechanisms, not just military presence. Whether Manila escalates its response — or turns to ASEAN and the International Court of Arbitration — will shape the next chapter of this long-running dispute.
